candidates.description: Rewrite the overdue query to join the active FeeSchedule and compute lateFee in the SELECT, returning OverdueInvoiceDto directly, removing the per‑row loop and the extra FeeSchedule query.
candidates.predicted_effect: SQL statements per request drop from ~101 (1 invoice query + ~100 feeSchedule queries) to 2 (single join query and no per‑row calls)
candidates.sql_before: SELECT i.id, c.name, i.amount, i.due_date FROM invoice i JOIN customer c ON c.id = i.customer_id WHERE i.status = %s ORDER BY i.due_date ASC, i.id ASC LIMIT %s, %s
candidates.sql_after: SELECT i.id, c.name, i.amount, i.due_date, i.amount * (fs.rate_percentage/100) AS late_fee FROM invoice i JOIN customer c ON c.id = i.customer_id JOIN fee_schedule fs ON fs.active = true WHERE i.status = %s ORDER BY i.due_date ASC, i.id ASC LIMIT %s, %s
what_could_break: If more than one FeeSchedule row has active = true the join could duplicate invoice rows; the business rule assumes exactly one active schedule.
The JPQL constructor expression must match the OverdueInvoiceDto constructor signature; mismatches cause runtime errors.
Changing the query may affect the execution plan; however the fee_schedule table is tiny (3 rows) so the join cost is negligible.
